key.title: I Learned to See Buildings Differently
key.main_idea: Saptarshi Kapri explains how his path from chemistry to architecture, and the hard early years of Karukrit Designs, taught him that architecture is about people experiencing buildings. He learned that good design is not enough: many building problems begin quietly in unclear decisions, so important choices should be resolved before construction whenever reasonably possible.

key_lessons.text: Architecture is not only about buildings; it is about people experiencing buildings.
key_lessons.source_snippet: It was about people experiencing buildings.

key_lessons.text: Clients need more than a beautiful drawing. They are trusting years of savings to a result they cannot yet see.
key_lessons.source_snippet: They were being asked to place years of savings behind a promise whose result they could not yet see.

key_lessons.text: Making every available project count builds credibility and, above all, pattern recognition.
key_lessons.source_snippet: But the most valuable thing we accumulated was not square footage. It was pattern recognition.

key_lessons.text: Good design can still become a difficult project if people understand it differently, so check what each conversation communicated.
key_lessons.source_snippet: A thoughtful design can still become a difficult project if the people involved understand it differently.

key_lessons.text: Problems often begin quietly in sentences like "We can decide that later." Ask what needs deciding now so it is not improvised later.
key_lessons.source_snippet: What needs to be decided now so that we do not have to improvise it later?

key.takeaway: Before construction starts, resolve every important decision you reasonably can. Quiet early conversations save loud problems on site.

quick_check.question: According to the author, where do many building problems really begin?
options: In unclear decisions and assumptions made before work starts
Only in poor workmanship on site
In choosing an unusual design style
quick_check.simpler_explanation: The author noticed that problems often start with small things like "We can decide that later" or an unclear scope. These seem harmless at first, but they cause trouble on site later.

reflection_questions: In your own home or project, which decision have you been putting off with "we can decide that later"?
Who is involved in your project, and might any of them understand the plan differently from you?
What would help you feel confident trusting a professional with years of your savings?

complete.main_idea: Saptarshi Kapri explains how his path from chemistry to architecture, and the hard early years of Karukrit Designs, taught him that architecture is about people experiencing buildings. He learned that good design is not enough: many building problems begin quietly in unclear decisions, so important choices should be resolved before construction whenever reasonably possible.

sections.heading: From chemistry to architecture
sections.explanation: The author began as a Chemistry Honours student in Kolkata, drawn to sketching, painting and making things. Architecture became the bridge between that creative instinct and building something real. What fascinated him was how a line on a drawing could decide where someone walks every morning.

examples.source_snippet: A drawing could become a room.

sections.heading: Starting before feeling ready
sections.explanation: Karukrit Designs began in 2018 with ambition but few landmark projects. Clients liked the ideas yet hesitated to trust a young practice with large projects. Over time he understood why: they were risking years of savings on a result they could not yet see.

examples.source_snippet: They were being asked to place years of savings behind a promise whose result they could not yet see.

sections.heading: Rebuilding and pattern recognition
sections.explanation: When his co-founder left and COVID arrived, survival became the priority. Instead of waiting for one big break, the studio made each smaller project count. The most valuable thing gained was pattern recognition: every project showed how office decisions played out on site.

examples.source_snippet: But the most valuable thing we accumulated was not square footage. It was pattern recognition.

sections.heading: Looking past the photograph
sections.explanation: A master's degree in Industrial Design shifted his attention to materials, manufacturing, usability and ageing. He began judging homes by the experience that continues after the photograph, not by one impressive wall.

examples.source_snippet: I began asking what happens after an object has been admired.

sections.heading: When good design is not enough
sections.explanation: A thoughtful design can still go wrong if people understand it differently. He learned to check what conversations had actually communicated: an idea may need a drawing, a technical point may need plain language, an approval may need a written record.

sections.heading: The problems that begin quietly
sections.explanation: He noticed recurring gaps: construction starting before the design was resolved, budgets left unspoken, familiar contractors appointed without a clear scope. Sentences like "We can decide that later" felt harmless. The question that stayed with him: what needs to be decided now so it is not improvised later?

examples.text: One of the sentences he learned to question.

sections.heading: The house before the house
sections.explanation: Families want to see walls rising, but quiet drawing reviews and budget meetings are part of building too. Every important decision that can reasonably be resolved before execution deserves that chance. This belief is why the book was written.
